fields.v: Zeng, Z., Li, Y., Xie, R., Ye, W., Zhang, S. (2025). Benchmarking and Studying the LLM-based Agent System in End-to-End Software Development. arXiv:2511.04064v1 [cs.SE], 6 Nov 2025. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2511.04064
Preprint — arXiv:2511.04064v1; no published venue found (pages carry the ACM template placeholder 'Conference'17, Washington, DC' and running head 'Trovato et al.')
Peking University, Beijing, China (all five authors)

Proposes an evaluation method; secondary: Compares — E2EDevBench (50 recent PyPI projects, requirements-only input) with a hybrid evaluation (test migration plus LLM requirement verification), and a controlled comparison of three agent workflows (single, developer-tester, designer-developer-tester) built on one SWE-agent foundation with two Gemini models

No SDD approach named. Authors' workflow configurations on SWE-agent (version not stated): SDAgent-Single (one agent: read requirements, implement, write and run tests, debug); SDAgent-DT (Developer agent then Tester agent); SDAgent-DDT (Designer agent writes a design document, then Developer, then Tester; 'design-implement-verify' waterfall)

Input: a requirements document per project (LLM-drafted from source code and README with a predefined template, then manually reviewed). SDAgent-DDT: a detailed project design document produced by the Designer agent; agents in all workflows write their own tests

Single: read requirements, implement, write tests, run, debug until tests pass. DT: develop (no tests), then test and debug. DDT: design, develop (from design document plus requirements), test and verify. Sequential hand-off between agents
None during agent runs (autonomous, max 200 steps). Humans only in benchmark construction (manual review of requirements documents) and in validating the judge
Full workflow of each authors' configuration, autonomously, from a requirements document; no SDD approach run

Not classifiable (no SDD approach; authors' wording: SDAgent-DDT simulates 'a more classical design-implement-verify waterfall workflow'; its design document resembles a spec-first plan but the authors do not use SDD terms)
New project: implement a whole repository from a requirements document only (no tests or skeleton given)
50 projects (10 per quarter, Q1 2024 to Q1 2025); reference repositories average 19.2 files, 2,011.5 LOC, 119.7 tests. Generated code 209-533 lines and 3.5-13.7 files on average per configuration
Python packages from PyPI (more than five source files, pytest test suite, no external API calls or hard-to-get dependencies); application domains Not stated
N/A (autonomous agents). Judge validation by three computer science graduate students
Tokens sent (M), tokens generated (K), cost (USD), agent steps per project (Table 3)

Implementation Rate (ImplRate): requirements unanimously judged implemented in three LLM assessments over all requirements (including inconclusive); Pass-Rate of tests (agent's own tests plus tests migrated from the original project)
None
None

Code lines and files generated; line and branch coverage of test suites (Table 2); judge agreement with humans (Pearson, pairwise agreement); run-to-run overlap of implemented requirements (Venn, 3 runs); step of first test writing; taxonomies of unimplemented requirements and failure root causes (Tables 4-5); performance by release quarter (leakage check)

Automatic: a Test Migration Agent (single-agent setup, Gemini-2.5-Pro) adapts the original project's tests to the generated code without modifying it; tests run in a sandbox; Gemini-2.5-Pro judges each requirement implemented/not implemented three times (unanimity required); tokens, cost, steps logged. Manual: judge validated against three graduate students on 10 projects (546 requirements); 1,000 unimplemented requirements classified by LLM pre-annotation then human refinement

Success criterion: none stated by the authors for a configuration, so quality and cost verdicts for every entry: no criterion stated by the authors. Values (Table 3): Impl-Req / Unimpl-Req / ImplRate; tests passed / failed / pass rate; tokens sent / generated; cost; steps. (1) SDAgent-Single + SWE-agent + Gemini-2.5-Flash: 27.14 / 23.32 / 48.46%; 42.35 / 12.96 / 76.57%; 20.90M / 161.24K; $6.67; 152.74 steps. (2) SDAgent-Single + SWE-agent + Gemini-2.5-Pro: 25.14 / 21.86 / 42.97%; 28.58 / 8.92 / 76.21%; 4.96M / 28.45K; $6.48; 80.12. (3) SDAgent-DT + Flash: 26.60 / 19.30 / 45.47%; 28.04 / 9.16 / 75.38%; 19.14M / 192.37K; $6.22; 90.60. (4) SDAgent-DT + Pro: 31.30 / 16.14 / 53.50%; 31.34 / 7.86 / 79.95%; 5.24M / 49.65K; $7.05; 77.36. (5) SDAgent-DDT + Flash: 12.82 / 31.88 / 22.63%; 25.57 / 12.49 / 67.18%; 18.27M / 151.64K; $5.86; 108.06. (6) SDAgent-DDT + Pro: 19.18 / 27.56 / 32.79%; 26.74 / 15.52 / 63.27%; 3.60M / 34.62K; $4.85; 86.16

Tasks: 50 E2EDevBench projects. Configurations: 3 workflows x 2 models (Gemini-2.5-Pro, Gemini-2.5-Flash). Baseline: SDAgent-Single (single agent). Held constant: SWE-agent foundation and toolset, temperature 0.2, max 200 steps, requirements document, sandbox, evaluator (Gemini-2.5-Pro). Acceptance: migrated original tests plus LLM requirement verification (3 assessments, unanimity). Repetitions: three independent runs for the Pro configurations (run overlap); whether Table 3 values are means over runs Not stated. Human intervention: none

Workflow matters: SDAgent-DT best mean ImplRate 49.48% (Pro 53.50%), Single 45.72%, DDT lowest 27.71%; authors attribute DDT's drop to errors in the design document propagating downstream, and Single's to interleaved code-test loops (first test at step 11.56 vs 27.96 for DT). Flash matched or beat Pro on ImplRate (Single: 48.46% vs 42.97%) at about four times the tokens sent. Cost per project $4.85-$7.05. Across three runs DT jointly fulfilled 796 requirements, 526 by one run only. No leakage drop on 2025-Q1 projects (42% vs 40%). Failures: missing features 32.4%, incorrect implementation 34.1%; root causes task planning 55.8%, execution 38.6%, verification 5.7%. No significance tests

Distinguished workflows (27.71% to 49.48% mean ImplRate); judge agreement with humans comparable to inter-human agreement (pairwise 76.7-84.4% vs 78.4-88.1%; Pearson 0.62-0.67); three runs showed a large common core but many run-specific successes. Limitations stated: possible implementation errors in the unified framework; only two Gemini models; reliance on LLM judge (validated on 10 projects)

Limitations: possible implementation errors in the authors' framework; only Gemini-2.5-Pro and Flash; benchmark quality depends on human-revised requirements; LLM-judge reliability. Gaps: agents fulfil only about half of requirements; main bottleneck is planning and requirement comprehension (omission, misinterpretation) and weak self-verification; premature self-submission by stronger models; cost-effective best-of-N aggregation; better agent orchestration and task decomposition

Inconsistencies: text says 'SDAgent-Single achieves the highest requirement implementation rate (49.48%), outperforming SDAgent-Single (45.72%)', but 49.48% is SDAgent-DT (p. 7); Fig. 4 legend 'SDAgent-D (Avg: 11.56)' for SDAgent-Single (p. 7); text says DDT's Dev and Test agents are 'configured identically to those of the SDAgent-Single', which by the workflow descriptions should be SDAgent-DT (p. 5, 8); 'partially implemented (21.7%)' in text vs 18.1% in Table 4 (p. 9); core-capability failures '5.6%' in text vs 3.2% for Technical Capability Bottleneck in Table 5 (5.6% is Architectural Design Flaw) (p. 9-10); Table 2 calls the agent's own tests 'Original Tests' and the migrated original-project tests 'Extended Tests' (p. 6); broken figure reference 'Figure ??' (p. 6); abstract says 'approximately 50%' while best mean is 49.48% and best single configuration 53.50%. Table 3 read from garbled text extraction, check against the PDF. Data: setup at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/E2EDevStudy-6C70 (p. 10-11). No pre-registration. Programming language: Python
